data_quality_assurance:
Several data quality assurance procedures will be implemented throughout the research process. Standardised data collection protocols will be used to ensure consistency across participants. Data will be collected using validated psychometric instruments and computerized assessment systems.
During data entry and processing, datasets will be checked for completeness, consistency, and potential outliers. Automated checks and manual verification procedures will be applied to identify missing values, implausible responses, and data entry errors.
Prior to analysis, data cleaning procedures will be conducted, including verification of variable coding, scale reliability checks, and documentation of all processing steps. These procedures ensure accuracy, reproducibility, and overall data integrity.
dataset.description: This dataset includes anonymized questionnaire data collected from athletes participating in a longitudinal and cross-cultural study conducted in Latvia, Lithuania, and Taiwan. The data are gathered at multiple time points during the sports season (pre-season, mid-season, and post-season) to assess key psychological indicators, including sleep quality, burnout symptoms, perceived social support, mental toughness, and sport-related anxiety. The dataset is used to examine changes in athletes’ psychological adaptation over time and to support cross-cultural comparisons while ensuring ethical standards and data protection.

distribution.title:
The purpose of the data collection is to systematically monitor changes in athletes’ psychological states throughout the sports season in order to support the objectives of the project “From Monitoring to Action: A Longitudinal and Cross-Cultural Approach to Athletes’ Psychological Adaptation Throughout the Sports Season”. The data are generated through standardized psychological questionnaires administered at multiple time points (pre-season, mid-season, and post-season) to capture longitudinal changes and enable cross-cultural comparisons between athletes in Latvia, Lithuania, and Taiwan.
The data originate directly from primary data collection involving voluntary participants and are used to identify patterns of psychological adaptation, mental fatigue, and resilience. The collected data will be useful for researchers, sport psychologists, coaches, and sports science professionals, contributing to evidence-based psychological support strategies and athlete well-being.

dataset.title: Survey_data

data_quality_assurance:
Several data quality assurance procedures will be implemented throughout the research process. Standardised testing protocols will be applied to ensure consistent administration of the Vienna Test System (VTS) across all participants. The VTS is a computerized assessment system that automatically records responses with high temporal precision, reducing the risk of manual data entry errors.
Test administration will follow standardized instructions and controlled testing conditions. Data exported from the VTS software will be checked for completeness, consistency, and potential outliers. Automated system-generated records will be reviewed to identify missing values or implausible results.
Prior to statistical analysis, additional data verification and cleaning procedures will be conducted, including inspection of variable coding, identification of extreme values, and documentation of all data processing steps. These procedures ensure accuracy, reproducibility, and overall data integrity.
dataset.description:
This dataset includes anonymized psychophysiological data collected from athletes in Latvia and Taiwan. In Latvia, data are generated using the Vienna Test System (VTS) to assess reaction time, attention, and stress tolerance through standardized computerized tests. In Taiwan, psychophysiological data are collected through heart rate variability (HRV) monitoring using wearable devices to assess physiological stress and recovery patterns across the sports season.
The purpose of this dataset is to provide objective indicators of athletes’ psychophysiological functioning and to complement self-reported psychological measures. The data support longitudinal analyses of adaptation and recovery processes and enable cross-cultural comparisons between different measurement approaches used within the project.

distribution.title:
The purpose of the psychophysiological data collection is to obtain objective indicators of athletes’ cognitive and physiological functioning in order to support the project’s objectives related to monitoring psychological adaptation across the sports season. These data provide objective measures that complement self-reported psychological assessments and enable a more comprehensive analysis of athletes’ adaptation processes.
The data are generated through primary data collection using standardized psychophysiological measurement tools in different national research contexts.
In Latvia, psychophysiological data are collected using the Vienna Test System (VTS), a computerized assessment system used to measure reaction time, attention, cognitive processing speed, and stress tolerance. In Taiwan, physiological data are generated through heart rate variability (HRV) monitoring using wearable devices to assess physiological stress regulation and recovery patterns.
Together, these data allow for longitudinal monitoring of athletes’ adaptation processes and enable cross-cultural comparisons within the project.

dataset.title: Psychophysiological_data

dmp.description: This longitudinal and cross-sectional study aims to develop a comprehensive athlete monitoring approach to assess changes in the psychological state of athletes (aged 18–25) throughout the sports season, considering sport-specific demands and competition phases. By systematically tracking key psychological (sleep quality and risk of sleep disorders, perceived burnout, perceived social support, mental toughness, and sport-related anxiety) and psychophysiological indicators (reaction time, attention, stress resistance, heart rate variability, and biofeedback parameters) at critical time points (pre-season, mid-season and post-season), this study will identify seasonal fluctuations in stress, peak performance periods and mental fatigue. The findings will facilitate the early detection of mental fatigue and burnout risks, enabling the implementation of targeted intervention strategies to enhance athlete well-being, resilience and performance. Additionally, this study will examine how different sports (open-skill and closed-skill disciplines) influence psychological adaptation and resilience, providing data-driven insights to refine mental preparation strategies. Conducted in Latvia, Lithuania and Taiwan, the research will enable cross-cultural comparisons of athletes' mental states, training loads and psychological adaptation mechanisms, contributing to a broader understanding of psychological preparedness in diverse training environments. By integrating psychological assessments with psychophysiological indicators (biofeedback analysis, the Vienna Test System battery, HRV (heart rate variability) monitoring and qualitative interviews) the study will produce scientifically validated recommendations for coaches, athletes and sports professionals. This represents a significant innovation. The results will support the development of evidence-based psychological training protocols and resilience-building strategies, ensuring alignment with sport periodization principles.
dmp.ethical_issues_description:
The research involves the collection of personal data from participants. Although all datasets used for analysis and sharing will be anonymised, the initial stages of data collection may include personal or potentially identifiable information. Therefore, ethical and legal considerations related to personal data protection and confidentiality apply.
All procedures will comply with institutional ethical guidelines and the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). Participants will provide informed consent prior to participation, and personal identifiers will be removed during the anonymisation process before data are shared or archived.
As the project involves collaboration between multiple research institutions, potential risks related to data sharing between partners are recognised. To mitigate these risks, only anonymised or pseudonymised datasets necessary for analysis will be shared through secure data transfer systems, and access will be limited to authorised project researchers.
